title: The U.S. Is Highly Vulnerable to Cyber Threats From China. Here’s What It Should Do | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Adam Segal argues U.S. critical infrastructure has never been more exposed to Chinese cyber operations, with China's cyber apparatus now rivaling America's and AI coding/cyber models accelerating offense. He summarizes a CFR study-group report with eighteen recommendations along four lines: shared visibility, cost imposition, infrastructure resilience, and rebuilt federal capacity.

themes.theme: CFR report: four lines of effort

insights.claim: A yearlong CFR study group with government, military and private-sector experts produced a report with eighteen recommendations, some of which impose costly burdens on industry, expand government authorities, or risk retaliation from Beijing.
insights.speaker: Adam Segal
insights.so_what: Signals potential new cybersecurity compliance costs for critical-infrastructure operators and retaliation risk for firms exposed to China.
insights.locator: The report includes eighteen specific recommendations

insights.claim: The U.S. government has poor visibility into Chinese cyber activity and should fix it through deeper private-sector integration, targeted sensing and automated threat sharing.
insights.speaker: Adam Segal
insights.so_what: Threat-intelligence and sensing vendors are positioned as government partners.
insights.locator: Build shared visibility into Chinese campaigns

insights.claim: U.S. offensive cyber operations should focus on degrading Chinese campaigns and their enabling infrastructure to buy time for structural reforms, alongside credible economic, diplomatic and cyber responses.
insights.speaker: Adam Segal
insights.so_what: A more aggressive U.S. cyber posture raises escalation and retaliation risk for U.S. firms.

insights.claim: Making networks easier and cheaper to defend requires shifting incentives that produce insecure technology products, restructuring internet infrastructure not built for security, and making AI a lasting defensive advantage, enabling baseline cybersecurity requirements for critical infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Adam Segal
insights.so_what: Secure-by-design liability and baseline mandates would raise costs for vendors of insecure products and boost security spend.

insights.claim: None of the recommendations can work without an empowered federal government able to set strategy, collaborate operationally with every sector, and hire and retain technical experts in civilian and military roles.
insights.speaker: Adam Segal
insights.so_what: Federal cyber workforce and capacity is a bottleneck; watch budget and hiring moves at cyber agencies.

insights.claim: The U.S. retains cyber advantages in the strength of its technology companies, alliance networks and economic tools.
insights.speaker: Adam Segal
insights.so_what: U.S. tech firms are central to national cyber strategy, implying public-private partnership demand.
